name: The Early American Republic and Its Letters
description: The writing of the American nation between the adoption of the Constitution and the Jacksonian settlement: the didactic and topographical verse of the Federalist clergy, the epic ambition of the American Musa, the sermon and the lecture, the political and educational tract, the dictionary and the grammar, and the first American reviews and magazines.
historical_context: The contest between Federalists and Republicans, the debates over the Alien and Sedition Acts, the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, the Embargo and the War of 1812, the Missouri agitation of 1819-21, the Erie Canal and the growth of the western lands, and the spread of common-school education and of Unitarian and evangelical theology all made the definition of a national literature an explicit political task. Yale and the Connecticut clergy, Philadelphia printing and the Boston monthlies supplied the institutions, and Noah Webster's spelling book and dictionary pursued a national language.
aesthetic_principles: The belief that a new nation owed itself an epic and a literature of instruction; the use of the didactic poem, the topographical description, and the hymn and sermon to teach republican virtue and Christian taste; a self-conscious Americanism in subject and in diction; and, in the reviews, an argument for an American criticism independent of Edinburgh and London.
defining_characteristics: The didactic and topographical poem (Timothy Dwight's Greenfield Hill, 1794); the revised revolutionary epic (Joel Barlow's The Columbiad, 1807); the denominational sermon and the theological lecture; the school grammar, spelling book and dictionary; the review and the monthly magazine; the political pamphlet and the fourth-debate speech; the biography and the memoir of the founding generation.
historical_significance: It created the institutions and the vocabulary of an American literature, and its argument about a national language, a national epic and a national criticism set the terms on which the later American writing of the 1830s and 1840s defined itself against Europe.

name: Charles Brockden Brown and the American Gothic
description: The tales and periodicals of Charles Brockden Brown and the American experiment in gothic and empirical fiction that followed them: stories of yellow fever, of sleep-walking, of secret witnesses and of religious and political delusion, set in the American cities and backcountries rather than in ruined castles.
historical_context: Brown wrote in Philadelphia in the years of the yellow fever epidemics of 1793 and 1798, of the French revolutionary controversy and the Alien and Sedition Acts, and of the decline of Federalist hopes. He edited the Monthly Magazine and American Review (1799-1800) and the American Register (1803-1806), and his theory of the tale as a vehicle for the analysis of mind and motive rests on Godwin's Political Justice, on Rousseau, and on the American empirical and medical writing of his friends.
aesthetic_principles: The romance of real life, with incident explained by the analysis of mind; the substitution of the American city, frontier and epidemic for the feudal castle; the use of mystery, error and mistaken evidence as the engine of plot; a moral and political seriousness about credulity, delusion and the abuse of confidence.
defining_characteristics: The epidemic tale (Arthur Mervyn); the sleep-walking and pursuit narrative of the western frontier (Edgar Huntly); the tale of secret witness and concealed motive (Ormond); the tale of religious delusion and its victims (Wieland, 1798); the editorial and review prose on the uses of fiction.
historical_significance: Brown is the first American novelist of importance and the inventor of an American gothic that dispenses with the castle and the superstition of the Old World while keeping its machinery of terror and mystery; his work is the origin of the American romance of delusion, pursuit and epidemic that runs through Poe, Hawthorne and later American fiction.

name: The Knickerbocker Group and the American Sketch
description: Washington Irving, his collaborators and imitators, and the forms they made American: the comic national history, the essay and character sketch, the German-derived tale of the supernatural in a colonial setting, and the traveller's romance.
historical_context: The Salmagundi Papers (1807-08), written by Irving with his brother Peter and James Kirke Paulding, satirised the manners and politics of New York; A History of New York by Diedrich Knickerbocker (1809) gave the state a mock-national past. Irving's English years, the Sketch Book published in parts (1819-20), and his subsequent travel writings made him the first American writer accepted in Britain, while the 'Knickerbocker' name became the label of a New York school that included Paulding, Fitz-Greene Halleck and Joseph Rodman Drake.
aesthetic_principles: Humour and gentle satire in place of invective; the adopted persona and the fictional editor as the means of national self-description; the association of the American landscape with Dutch and colonial legend; the tale of the supernatural told with an ironic and social eye; the essay of manners, travel and reminiscence as the proper prose of a new nation.
defining_characteristics: The mock chorography and comic national history; the periodical sketch and character (the Crayon papers, 'Rip Van Winkle', 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow'); the Germanizing ghost tale and the colonial haunted landscape; the traveller's romance of Spain and the Alhambra; the society satire of the magazine and the annual.
historical_significance: Irving gave American prose fiction its first international reputation and fixed the short tale and the sketch as characteristic American forms; the Knickerbocker group created the first self-conscious school of American letters, and the 'Knickerbocker' legend supplied New York with a usable colonial past.

name: Cooper and the American Romance of Forest and Sea
description: James Fenimore Cooper's invention of an American romance in two settings, the frontier and the ocean: the tale of the Indian, the settler and the last of a people, and the narrative of the ship, the crew and the naval action.
historical_context: Cooper began with a novel of manners composed to win a wager, Precaution (1820), and turned at once to the revolutionary spy tale (The Spy, 1821) and to the frontier fiction of the French and Indian war and its aftermath (The Pioneers, 1823; The Last of the Mohicans, 1826; The Prairie, 1827). The long sea service that gave him his material ended with his return from Italy and the copyright dispute with British publishers, while the Jacksonian argument over Indian removal formed the political background of his later frontier tales.
aesthetic_principles: The romance of a people and a landscape rather than of a single society; the heroic frontier figure at odds with law and with settlement; the use of the Indian as the emblem of an expiring nation; the sea as a scene of discipline, fellowship and courage; the deliberate mixture of historical fact, topographical description and adventure.
defining_characteristics: The frontier tale and the 'Leatherstocking' sequence; the sea and naval narrative with its technical authenticity and its study of authority; the colonial spy and revolution tale; the traveller's book on American manners and institutions; the preface and introductory essay defending or explaining the romance.
historical_significance: Cooper made the American forest, the Indian and the sea the great subjects of American fiction and set the pattern of the frontier romance that later American writing inherited and reacted against; his naval narratives founded the American sea story, and his tale of Natty Bumppo remains the founding myth of the American novel.

name: Bryant and the American Nature Lyric
description: The American nature lyric and the public verse that William Cullen Bryant and his contemporaries made: meditative blank verse on death, landscape and the solitude of the observer, with the poem of national occasion and the ballad of the American scene.
historical_context: Bryant's 'Thanatopsis' appeared in the Monthly Anthology in 1811, when he was still a teenager in Massachusetts, and his removal to New York and his long editorship of a daily paper made him the central figure of American letters before the civil war. The occasional verses of the war of 1812, Joseph Rodman Drake's 'The Culprit Fay' (1819), Fitz-Greene Halleck's narrative and lyric poems of the 1820s and the annuals' supply of verse created a public for an American lyric of nature and memory.
aesthetic_principles: The didactic and meditative use of natural scene, in the manner of Thomson and of the British blank-verse school; a grave and consolatory treatment of death and the prospect of the future; the conviction that poetry should be at once popular and instructive; the national or commemorative occasion as a legitimate ground for verse.
defining_characteristics: The blank-verse meditation on landscape and death; the poem of the bird, the stream and the solitude; the Indian and frontier elegy; the national ode and the commemorative lyric; the editorial and critical essay on poetry written by poets.
historical_significance: Bryant established the American nature lyric and, as editor and critic, the authority of the man of letters in American public life; his 'Thanatopsis' was the first American poem widely read in Europe, and his example made the meditative lyric on American scenery the country's characteristic Romantic mode.
